text: A conclave is a closed meeting of a small group of people who have the standing to decide something. The word comes from the Latin for “with a key”, because the cardinals who choose a new pope are locked in until they agree, and journalists now borrow it for any private gathering of senior figures working out a position. Here it is the biologists who met in Singapore — not an open conference, but the handful of people who actually work on mirror life.

To promulgate something is to issue it officially and publicly, so that from that moment it counts as the formal position of whoever issued it: a government promulgates a law, a committee promulgates its findings. It is stronger than announce, and the force of it is the authority standing behind it. When the Singapore recommendations are promulgated in a report, they stop being private views and become the field's stated line.

To disabuse someone is to rid them of a belief that is wrong, almost always in the frame “disabuse someone of” an idea. Hiding inside it is abuse in its older sense of misuse — a person taken in by a false idea has been ill-used by it, and disabusing them undoes that. Deepa Agashe brought measurements of soil, blood and gut contents to the meeting precisely to take away the doubt that mirror life could feed itself.

Saying biology is handed has nothing to do with giving something to someone: it means its molecules come in two versions that are mirror images, like your left and right hands, which are built from the same parts and still cannot be laid on top of each other. Handedness is the noun for that property. The article's whole subject is what would happen if someone built life with the opposite handedness.

To synthesise something is to build it up from simpler parts by chemical steps, rather than extracting it from something that already exists; the noun is synthesis. Chemists synthesise drugs and dyes, and the much harder ambition here is synthesising a whole living cell from scratch. Note the British spelling with an s — American writing uses synthesize.

The confines of something are the limits that hold it in — walls, a boundary, a space you cannot get out of. Escaping the confines of the lab is the phrase carrying the article's entire fear. As a verb, confine means to keep something inside those limits.

Keen here means eager or very willing, the common British sense as in “keen to help”. It is not the other meaning of keen, sharp, as in a keen blade or a keen sense of smell. Scientists being keen to nip the research in the bud means they badly want it stopped early.

Something arbitrary is settled by choice or convenience rather than by any underlying reason, so it could just as easily have gone the other way. Calling the left-and-right labelling of molecules an arbitrary convention means chemists had to pick one, and did — nothing in nature says which is which. The word often carries a complaint, as in an arbitrary rule or an arbitrary deadline.

A convention here is an agreed way of doing things that everyone in a field sticks to, not a large meeting, which is the other sense of the word. Driving on the right, writing dates day-first or month-first, and calling one molecule left-handed are all conventions: useful, binding, and not facts about nature. Which sense is meant is usually clear from what follows it.

A backbone, outside anatomy, is the long central chain that everything else hangs off. In DNA and RNA the sugar molecules link into exactly such a chain, with the genetic letters attached along its length. Writers use the word the same way for the main structure of a network or an organisation.

In chemistry a sugar is any of a family of small carbon-based molecules, not just the white stuff in the bowl; glucose, fructose and ribose are all sugars. Besides being fuel, they do structural work, since ribose and deoxyribose form the backbones of RNA and DNA. That is how the article can say life's sugars are right-handed while its amino acids are left-handed.

A paper is a formal write-up of a piece of research, published in a journal so that other scientists can check it and build on it. The 2024 paper the article keeps returning to is one specific published argument with named authors, which is why those authors can still be quoted about it years later. Nothing to do with the material you write on.

Curiosity carries two senses in this article. One is the ordinary urge to find out; the other is an oddity, a strange thing of no real importance, which is what mirror life looked like at first. When someone calls an idea “a curiosity rather than a threat”, they mean it is interesting and harmless.

To posit something is to put it forward as a claim to be argued about, without having proved it yet. Scientists and philosophers posit a mechanism and then go looking for evidence for or against it. The authors posited that a mirror bacterium would slip past immune systems: a reasoned proposal, not a demonstrated fact.

Unchecked means with nothing holding it back — no brake, no limit, no opposing force. A bacterial population normally is checked, by predators, viruses and immune responses, so reproducing unchecked is exactly what makes a mirror organism frightening. The word fits anything that grows without resistance, from a rumour to a fire.

Principal means main or most important, so the principal predators of bacteria are the ones doing most of the eating. Do not confuse it with principle, a rule or belief, which sounds identical; a school principal is called that because the job was originally the principal teacher. If you can swap in “main”, the spelling ending in -pal is the right one.

To metabolise something is to break it down chemically inside a living body and use it for energy or building material; the whole set of those reactions is called metabolism. Mirror life could not metabolise ordinary left-handed amino acids, because its enzymes would be shaped for the opposite hand. Spelled metabolize in American English.

Remote here means very unlikely, not far away: a remote possibility is one with only a slim chance of happening. The two senses share an idea of distance, except that a remote chance is far off in probability rather than in miles. The article's point is that making mirror life is a remote possibility today and may not stay remote for long.

Novel as an adjective means new, of a kind not seen before, so novel viruses are newly designed ones rather than stories in a book. It is the standard word in science writing for something genuinely unprecedented, as in a novel coronavirus. The noun and the adjective are the same word only by an accident of history.

Piecemeal means done bit by bit, in separate stages, rather than all at once. The article sets a piecemeal route to mirror life — converting a cell a little at a time — against the big-bang route of building one outright. The word often hints that the stop-start approach is the untidier one, though here it is simply the slower path.

A spud is a potato, an informal and mostly British word for it. The spud cell earned its nickname purely because it looks like one; potatoes have nothing to do with the science. Researchers name things this casually more often than you would expect.

In biology, to encode something is to carry the instructions for building it: a stretch of DNA encodes a protein, in the sense that the order of its chemical letters sets the order of that protein's parts. Seven plasmids encoding 36 enzymes means those loops of DNA hold the recipes for 36 of them. The same word covers any system where one pattern stands for another, like a code or a file format.

Respectively tells you to match two lists up in the order given: if A and B are X and Y respectively, then A is X and B is Y. The article says D-peptides and spiegelmers are opposite-handed proteins and nucleic acids respectively, so D-peptides are the proteins and spiegelmers the nucleic acids. Writers use it to avoid saying the same sentence twice.

Saying something happened proverbially means the writer is nodding at a well-known saying rather than making a fresh claim. The proverb here is “curiosity killed the cat”, a warning that poking into things can end badly. The joke is a grim one: this time curiosity might kill a good deal more than a cat.

To opine is to state an opinion, especially formally or in public. A government opines on another country's research; a scientist opined that her data settles a point. The word often carries a faint dryness, the writer quietly noting that an opinion is all it is.

Concrete here means specific and real rather than vague, so concrete action is a particular thing someone will actually do, as opposed to general concern. It is the standard opposite of abstract in writing about policy and argument. Nothing to do with the grey stuff in sidewalks, although the idea of something solid is shared.

To foreshadow something is to give an early hint of what is coming before it formally arrives. Dr Church foreshadowed the report's recommendations by sketching them in a talk months ahead of publication. In stories the same word describes an early clue that something is about to happen.

Scrutiny is close, careful, often suspicious examination — the kind of looking that is meant to catch something. DNA synthesis companies are already under scrutiny, meaning their orders get checked in case someone is assembling a dangerous pathogen. The verb is scrutinise.

A malefactor is a wrongdoer; the word is built from Latin parts meaning bad-doer, the exact opposite of a benefactor who does good. It is formal, a little old-fashioned, and usually reached for when a legal penalty is in view. Here the malefactors would be researchers who build mirror life in defiance of the rules.

Lest is a formal connective meaning “in case” or “for fear that” — you do something lest the bad thing happen. “Lest anyone have lingering doubts” simply means in case anyone still doubts. It is one of the few places English still uses an old subjunctive verb form, which is why it reads as have rather than has.

A telling detail or analogy is one that reveals something important — it tells you more than it looks able to. Calling Agashe's comparison a telling analogy means the comparison itself does real explaining. The everyday verb sense of telling is not involved.

Neotropical means belonging to the tropical Americas — Central and South America and the Caribbean — as opposed to the tropics of Africa or Asia. Cane toads are neotropical by origin, which is exactly why they are a disaster in Australia, where nothing evolved alongside them. Biologists divide the world into regions like this to talk about where species came from.

Tangible means able to be touched, and by extension real enough to point at. A tangible threat is one already doing damage rather than a possibility on paper. The article's argument is to act while the danger is still intangible, because by the time it is tangible it is too late.

A vested interest is a stake someone already holds in how something turns out — money, a job, a position they stand to lose. Vested itself means formally granted and now firmly held, as in rights vested in a person. The article's point is an encouraging one: because nobody yet makes money from mirror life, there are no vested interests lobbying to protect it.

To sway someone is to influence them enough to change what they do, literally to make them lean one way. Business lobbies and governments are swayed by money and strategic advantage, neither of which is yet in play here. The noun sway means that same influence, as in “under the sway of”.

A lobby is an organised group that pressures governments on behalf of an industry or a cause — the business lobbies, the farm lobby, the gun lobby. The name comes from people waiting in the lobby of a parliament to catch legislators on their way through. The hotel-entrance meaning is the same word, so the sense has to be read from context.

To avert something is to stop it before it happens by turning it aside: you avert a disaster, a crisis, a collision. It is the word of choice when harm is already on its way and action is still possible. Averting your eyes is the same turning-away idea applied literally.

forms: nip such research in the bud
text: To nip something in the bud is to stop it at the very start, before it can develop; the image is pinching off a flower bud so that it never opens. It is the standard English phrase for early, pre-emptive action. That is precisely what the biologists want done to mirror-life research.

To make something from scratch is to build it from basic ingredients, with no ready-made parts and no head start. Baking a cake from scratch rather than from a mix is the everyday version; synthesising a living cell from scratch is the extreme one. The phrase comes from a starting line scratched into the ground.

Something on the horizon is not here yet but is close enough to see coming. Biotechnologists can see synthetic cells on the horizon, meaning this is a real prospect rather than a fantasy. The opposite image is a distant prospect, nowhere in sight.

To hold a mirror to something is normally to show it to itself, revealing what it is really like. The article is playing on that, because a mirror cell would literally be a reflected version of ordinary biochemistry, reversed in every handed part. Writers often use a familiar phrase in its literal sense like this for effect.

To beg to differ is a polite, slightly stiff way of saying “I disagree”; the begging is old-fashioned courtesy, not pleading. The paper's authors begged to differ with everyone who thought mirror life a mere curiosity. It usually signals firm disagreement delivered mildly.

To advance by leaps and bounds is to improve very fast and in large jumps rather than steadily. Both leaps and bounds mean jumps, and doubling them up is pure emphasis, the way English does in “safe and sound”. Synthetic biology advancing by leaps and bounds is the reason the old fifteen-year estimate may be wrong.

So-called introduces the name people give something, often with a hint that the writer is only reporting the label rather than endorsing it. A so-called spud cell is a cell researchers nicknamed that. When the doubt is heavier, so-called comes close to sneering, so read the surrounding tone.

In principle means in theory, as far as the rules allow, with practical difficulties set aside — often with a quiet “but not yet in practice” behind it. Church's modified cells can in principle take right-handed amino acids, meaning nothing forbids it, not that it has been done at scale. The sibling phrase is in practice.

To beaver away is to work steadily and industriously at something over a long stretch, from the beaver's reputation for ceaseless dam-building. The 2024 paper's authors have been beavering away at persuading governments, which is slow and unglamorous work. Mostly British, and always approving.

A big beast, in British political and business writing, is a powerful player whose sheer weight makes it impossible to ignore. Calling China one of the field's big beasts means no agreement about mirror life can really work without it. The phrase began as a description of senior politicians.

To weed out is to go through a group and remove the unwanted members, the way a gardener pulls weeds from a bed. Psychological evaluations would be meant to weed out researchers likely to break the rules. The phrase always implies the removal is selective and deliberate.

Off-piste comes from skiing, where the piste is the marked, patrolled run, so going off-piste means leaving it for unmarked snow. Figuratively it means doing something outside the approved route, which here means a scientist ignoring agreed limits. The phrase keeps the skier's whiff of recklessness.

To resort to something is to fall back on it because the better option is unavailable; the phrase carries reluctance or last-ditch necessity. A mirror bacterium would not need to resort to chiral food, because unhanded nutrients would be plentiful enough. The holiday sense of resort is the same word — a place you turn to.

To run riot is to spread or behave with no restraint at all, as cane toads do across Australia. The phrase works for anything uncontrolled: weeds, a rumour, children left alone, an imagination. It is the everyday cousin of reproducing unchecked.

All the same means “even so”: it concedes the point just made and then pushes on anyway. Having granted that a mirror bioweapon would be unusable, the writer adds that, all the same, the warnings matter. Noticing these small concession phrases is how you follow the turns in an argument.

For lack of something means because that thing is missing — cane toads thrive in Australia for lack of predators able to eat them. It is a compact way of giving a cause by naming an absence. The close relative is “for want of”, as in “for want of a nail”.

Mirror life is the hypothetical kind of organism — probably a bacterium — built entirely from the opposite-handed versions of life's molecules: right-handed amino acids, left-handed sugars. Nothing like it exists, and the whole article is about whether it ever should. The name is literal, since such a cell would be a chemical reflection of ordinary life.

Chirality is the property of coming in two mirror-image forms that cannot be laid on top of each other, from the Greek kheir, meaning hand; a molecule with the property is chiral. It arises when a carbon atom holds four different attachments, which can be arranged in two ways. Chirality matters because molecules act by fitting together, and the wrong hand does not fit.

Achiral means not handed: the molecule is identical to its own mirror image, so there is only one version of it. Agashe's point was that soil, blood and gut contents are full of achiral nutrients, which ordinary and mirror organisms could both eat. The a- prefix meaning “not” turns up all over science, as in asymmetric and atypical.

Amino acids are the small molecules a cell strings together, in a particular order, to build proteins; about twenty are in common use, and DNA is what specifies the order. Each one is a carbon atom carrying three fixed attachments plus a variable fourth part that makes it the acid it is. That four-way arrangement is why nearly all of them are handed, and life uses the left-handed version.

Nucleic acids are the information molecules of life: DNA, which stores the instructions, and RNA, which carries and uses them. Each is a long chain of sugar units with chemical letters hanging off it, which is why the article mentions their sugar backbones. The name comes from the cell nucleus, where DNA was first found.

A tetrahedron is a four-cornered pyramid with triangular faces, so a tetrahedral arrangement means four things pointing out from a centre towards those corners. That is the shape a carbon atom's four bonds take, and it is the reason handedness exists at all: swap two of the four corners and you get a mirror image rather than a rotation. Flat arrangements cannot be handed this way.

Science here is not the subject but the name of a journal, one of the two most prestigious places in the world to publish research, alongside Nature. Saying a paper appeared in Science is itself a claim about how seriously the work was taken. Journals like it use peer review, meaning other specialists examined the work before it was published.

Through the Looking-Glass is Lewis Carroll's 1871 sequel to Alice in Wonderland, in which Alice steps into a mirror world where everything is reversed. Used as an adjective for mirror organisms it signals both the reversal and a hint of the absurd. It is one of those book titles that became an everyday phrase.

An amoeba is a single-celled organism that moves by pushing out blobs of itself and feeds by wrapping around smaller things and dissolving them; amoebae is the plural. They are among the main eaters of bacteria in soil and water. Because digesting depends on enzymes that fit what is being digested, a mirror bacterium might pass through one untouched.

A bacteriophage, or phage, is a virus that infects bacteria and nothing else; the name means bacteria-eater. It is a protein shell holding a loop of DNA, which docks onto one specific molecule on a bacterium's surface and pushes its DNA inside, after which the cell's own machinery assembles new phages until the cell splits open. Phages are the most numerous biological objects on Earth and a major reason bacterial populations stay in check.

Synthetic biology is the field that designs and builds biological parts and whole organisms rather than only studying existing ones: writing DNA sequences, assembling cells, engineering bacteria to manufacture drugs. It sits where molecular biology, chemistry and engineering meet. Its speed, now increased further by AI, is why mirror life has moved from thought experiment to a question of years.

The Big Bang is cosmology's name for the origin of the universe, and writers borrow it for anything that arrives all at once instead of gradually. A big-bang mirror cell would be built complete, in one go, rather than converted piece by piece. The contrast the article draws is big bang versus piecemeal.

George Church is a geneticist at Harvard Medical School and one of the best-known figures in synthetic biology, involved in much of the technology for reading and writing DNA. He co-authored the 2024 paper that raised the alarm, and his own lab's work on unusual amino acids is one of the steps towards mirror chemistry. When someone proposes restrictions on his own field, that carries particular weight.

A plasmid is a small loop of DNA that sits apart from a cell's main chromosome and can be copied and passed around; bacteria swap them, which is one way antibiotic resistance spreads. Because they are easy to design and insert, plasmids are the workhorse tool of genetic engineering. The spud cell carried seven of them in place of a proper genome.

An enzyme is a protein that speeds up one specific chemical reaction by holding the molecules involved in exactly the right position; almost nothing in a cell happens without one. That holding is purely a matter of shape, so an enzyme built for a left-handed molecule will not grip its right-handed twin. That single fact is why mirror life could not eat ordinary food.

D-peptides are short protein chains built from right-handed amino acids, and spiegelmers are the mirror-image equivalent of short nucleic acids — spiegel is German for mirror. Both exist today and some are in medical use, because a body's enzymes cannot break down the wrong-handed version, so the drug keeps working longer. They show that useful mirror molecules can be made without making mirror organisms.

A pathogen is anything that causes disease: a bacterium, a virus, a fungus or a parasite. The word groups them by what they do rather than by what they are, which is what makes screening DNA orders for pathogen sequences possible at all. Most bacteria are not pathogens; the dangerous ones are a small minority.

E. coli, short for Escherichia coli, is a bacterium that lives harmlessly in huge numbers in the human gut and is the most studied organism in biology — much of what is known about how bacteria work came from it. A few strains do cause illness, which is why it turns up in food-poisoning news. Agashe used it as the yardstick: if E. coli could live on unhanded food, a mirror bacterium probably could too.

An invasive species is one carried into a place it did not evolve in, where it spreads because the local predators, parasites and diseases are not adapted to it. Cane toads in Australia, zebra mussels in the Great Lakes and kudzu in the American south are the standard examples. The analogy to mirror life is exact and, as the article notes, discouraging: invasives are sometimes controlled, never eliminated.

A whistle-blower is an insider who reports wrongdoing inside their own organisation to people who can act on it. The idea matters because insiders are often the only ones who can see a violation, and because they risk their jobs doing it; many countries have laws protecting them. Incentivising whistle-blowers means paying or shielding them so that dangerous research is more likely to be reported.
